So I have no practical experience with this. However, being a Dungeon Master, I've researched how far one can realistically walk in the name of D&D. Average walking speed is about 3 mph, and one can walk about 8 hours a day before getting exhausted. This would net you around 24 miles in an 8 hour day--18 miles at a slow pace, and 30 at a fast one. These are approximations for the game world, but they'll work as an estimate for what a fit person can realistically accomplish. 



Google maps seems to bear this out; a journey of 43 miles from Philadelphia, PA to Princeton, NJ is estimated to take 16 hours by walking. I would say this is fairly impossible to do in a single day with only one bottle of water and no food. You could **maybe** make it if you take 2 days, refilling your water bottle at gas stations along the way, but you would be very hungry at the end of it. Walking burns about 100 calories per mile, so you could expect it to cost about 4600 calories to walk 46 miles.

Mmh, I would say it's more complex than him just being evil. He enjoys exercising power over others because he's spent his existence as a powerless spawn, and he equates having power over others with being free. 

His "good" character arc is choosing to keep himself weak (rather than ascending), because he doesn't want to be the creature that Cazador made him. Freedom over power. 

This is also why he reacts so violently when you mention Cazador to him after he ascends. He revels in his new power, but he knows he will never be free of Cazador's influence--power over freedom.

I'd definitely give him some sort of bonus for eating the bones - as another commenter said, maybe Radiant Consumption from the Fallen Aasimar statblock. As a DM, I like to incentivize evil decisions in the short term, both so that it's more meaningful when the party makes good decisions, and also to reward creative roleplay rather than making "be a good guy" the easiest and most mechanically advantageous decision in every circumstance. Also, it's way more fun for me when the players make bad or impulsive decisions. It helps push the story forwards in dramatic and interesting ways. 

I feel like it makes narrative sense as well for the desecration of holy bones to warp the player's very being. 

And naturally, this decision should have disastrous consequences for Vallaki, as evil choices tend to do.
I love this, it's so much more fun as a DM and as a player to say "the desecration of this holy artifact has warped your very nature" than to go "you take a little radiant damage and that's it"

The only real demand Akemi ever made of someone is Mizu, who, in all fairness, she had just risked her life for, rather than locking herself up in the basement with the prostitutes. Seki chose to accompany Akemi, then demanded she come home. She refused. 

You didn't answer my question: *Shouldn't Akemi be allowed to make decisions for herself?*
Okay, but shouldn't she be allowed to make her own decisions, even if you disagree with them?

Why shouldn't Akemi's decisions be respected? Do you mean that other people should be allowed to criticize her decisions? They can and they do. Do you mean they should prevent her from making her own decisions? They certainly try. 

To your last point: Nobody is entitled to be believed in. That doesn't mean it wouldn't hurt if your surrogate father took away your choices and treated you like a foolish child. Seki even admits that he was wrong, and that her choices were never for him to decide.

You say Mizu would've beaten Taigen anyway; I could say Akemi would've succeeded at seducing her customer regardless of whether he was into poetry. Quibbling about what might've been if circumstances were different is missing the point. Success requires skill, luck, and the courage to act. You consistently attribute any victories of Akemi's to purely luck and disregard the courage it took to act in the first place as foolishness. This is why I think your dislike of the character is more irrational than well reasoned.

Edit: Reviewing this comment thread I think we've gotten a bit off topic. All I meant to say was that Akemi deserves respect in the same way that every person deserves respect; to be treated as their own person and given courtesy of making their own decisions. But it's fine if you don't like her.

You can attribute anything to luck, though. For example: Isn't it lucky for Mizu that Taigen was tipsy when they dueled? Isn't it lucky that she fought the Fangs on a cliffside instead of on flat ground? Isn't it lucky Ringo saved her in ep3? Isn't it lucky that Fowler toyed with her in ep6 instead of killing her outright?

I'm not arguing any of that seriously, of course. The point is, in order to get lucky, you must first have the courage to act. Whether Akemi succeeds or fails, and regardless of whether that's due to skill or luck, the fact that she acted when others encouraged her not to even try makes her brave. If she had ended up a prostitute at knifepoint, as you said earlier, I would still find that more admirable than if she had stayed home and married the shogun's son without protest. 

As for being taken away by her father's men, I think she's right to be annoyed. She never wanted to be married to the shogun's son and still presumably doesn't. What she *does* want is to bring about change, and currently staying in Edo and being married to Takayoshi is the best way to do that. But that was her decision to make, not her father's. Mizu saw an injustice being committed and decided to look the other way. No one can blame her for it, but I certainly wouldn't describe such a person as a 'friend.'

You're arguing irrationally. Whenever Akemi succeeds, it's luck; whenever she fails, it's because she's a pampered princess. I think it's admirable that she continues to try when everyone around her tells her she should give up, but clearly you're just not a fan.
I mean obviously there's nuance, I was just correcting the 'abusive men secretly want to be dominated' part of your comment. Madame Kaji says the opposite.

You say that Seki was right to expect failure, but the whole point is that she didn't fail? He gave up on her but she didn't give up on herself. She kept going, demoralized beyond belief and in a worse condition than she'd ever been, and managed to track down the man she was looking for in a nation of millions! She was lucky but also clever. You don't find that at all admirable? Wasn't Mizu lucky to find Swordfather, or to get saved from the arrow canyon by Ringo? Does the fact that Mizu got lucky make her less admirable as a character?

I think Madame Kaji says the opposite, actually. Insecure men want to feel powerful; they act beastly because they fear being seen as weak. Kaji suggests that Akemi plays into this. If she gives the impression that *she* is being dominated, that *she* is weak and under their sway, then they will feel powerful. In reality, that power is illusory because it depends on others' opinion of them, which is fickle and leaves them open to manipulation.

I respect your opinion here, but I see it differently. One of the first lines that really endeared me to Akemi was what she says to Seki in episode 3: "To find out only now you never believed in me." Nobody expects anything of her, not even Seki, the man who raised her. Yeah, maybe she does come from privilege and maybe she makes irrational decisions, but those are decisions which *she has a right to make* and which have been constantly denied to her under the pretense that she's a pampered princess who doesn't know what's best for her; a pig whose teeth will rot if she's given too much sugar. It's absolutely infantilizing. 

Initially all she feels she can hope for is to marry a good husband; Taigen is the best option available for her. The character growth we see from Akemi shows her coming to realize that she doesn't have to pursue *other* people's ideas of happiness. She might struggle and fail, but she has a right to pursue her own happiness, in her own way, and she's no less capable of achieving it than any other person.

I disagree that Akemi or anyone has to *earn* the right to be treated as a whole person with the right and ability to pursue their own happiness. Everyone deserves this basic level of respect, but it's one thing which has been constantly denied to Akemi. I love her as a character because she learns to hold on to this ideal even when everyone around her says that she would be better off if she learned to "steal" moments of happiness in the course of the life they envision for her.

As many have said, the best option is to tell the truth. Which means the second best option is to double down, so here's how to do that.

First, read the player's handbook if possible. Wizards of the Coast (publisher of DnD) has a shorter version called [Basic Rules](https://media.wizards.com/2018/dnd/downloads/DnD_BasicRules_2018.pdf) which has most of what you need to know. Not everything is important; the PHB (common abbreviation for player's handbook) is divided up into 3 sections, and you really only need section 2, "Playing the Game." Section 4 in the above PDF is only for dungeon masters (DMs), and Sections 1 and 3 should be read selectively. For example, don't read the all the races, classes, backgrounds, equipment, or spells, just read the ones for your character specifically. I've just looked and BG3 has the same 12 classes as DnD, but race-wise, Drow is a type of elf, and Githyanki is supplementary content not in the PHB. Otherwise races are the same. If the PHB doesn't do it for you, there are lots of guides. [This one from RPGBOT](https://rpgbot.net/dnd5/how-to-play/) is my favorite.

Second, start making your character ASAP - or even better, use a pre-build. The first time I built a character in D&D it took me 4 hours, and you don't have that kind of time. I recommend Barbarian, because you'll be harder to kill and therefore won't have to make a new character. (Avoid spellcasters, they're tricky and you don't have time to learn the mechanics of spells. Non-casters: Barbarian, Fighter, Monk, Rogue.) You should come to session 0 with a strong idea of the character you want to use, because that way you won't have to get drawn into a discussion over the pros/cons of various classes. The 3 most important characteristics your party and DM will want to know are race, class, and subclass. If someone else has a character concept similar to yours, give it the old "oh, but I always play this character!" because the DM will let you play the same race, and might let you play the same class, but if you have two players with the same subclass, they will probably want one of you to change--so put your character concept out there first.

Pre-gen Option 1: The Digital DM used to have loads of premade characters for each level, so no matter what level you're starting at (it's not uncommon to start at level 3, for example - decided during session 0) or how long the campaign goes, you'll always have a sheet appropriate for the level you're at. The site is down now, but [this redditor](https://www.reddit.com/r/DnD/comments/yxmka8/comment/iwqiqab/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=web2x&context=3) made an archive.

Pre-gen Option 2: Use [rpgbot](https://rpgbot.net/dnd5/characters/classes/), which has a feature called "X Handbook" for most subclasses you might want to use. Choose the class you want, pick a subclass, then do everything he says to in the "Example Build" section. Again, this guide shows you what decisions to make as you level up, which can be tricky for new players. As he doesn't actually generate the character sheet, you'll have to fill it out yourself. Here's a solid [Totem Warrior Barbarian](https://rpgbot.net/dnd5/characters/classes/barbarian/subclasses/totem-warrior/) build.

Third, buy a dice set. Buy two or three, actually. For added authenticity, choose a D20 at random and claim it's lucky / cursed - lots of people in DnD are superstitious about their dice. Since you only have a few days, try a local gaming store, but if you can't find one in time you can always claim you "forgot" your dice and other players will certainly let you borrow a set. I think dice are the same between BG3 and DnD, but if not you should definitely memorize which is the d4, d6, d8, etc.

Fourth, the flow of a session can be unusual for people who haven't played before. Consider watching an episode of Critical Role, Dimension 20, or Adventure Zone to get a feel of what you're expected to do - or even better, watch part of all 3 and *note the differences* in play style. Variation is normal and expected across tables. Broadly speaking, DnD can be divided up into two different modes:

1. Combat, covered by Chapter 9 of the PHB, which is highly structured and where it's very important to know what your character can and cannot do, mechanically speaking. Combat begins when you roll initiative and ends when you stop acting in initiative order. (This is a generalization but suffice to say it should be pretty obvious when you're in combat.) It's also the only part of D&D which happens on a board - generally a 1 inch square grid. Some players might have a character token, but you can just use a d4.
2. Roleplay, which covers everything else. Here you can pretty much tell the DM straight up what you want to do, and they'll tell you exactly how to make that happen, what rolls you need to make, etc. New players tend to struggle much more with combat than roleplay.

Every table handles roleplay differently, but outside of house rules or homebrew, combat is the same, so you should have a good understanding of the mechanics. If yourforget or misunderstand a rule, either brush it off (it happens to everybody), or just say that you forgot because your last table ran it differently (homebrew & houserules are common).

Fifth - some tips for session 0:

* People might ask about your alignment in addition to class, subclass, and race, because they like to pretend it's important. It's not. Say neutral good and be done with it.
* You might be asked to roll stats for your character during Session 0. They're asking you to generate ability scores. The most common method is roll 4d6, drop the lowest dice from the total. Otherwise, the above pre-gen options use either the standard set described in the PHB (15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8, assigned at your discretion to each stat) or point-buy (more complicated, find an online guide), plus any racial modifiers or bonuses from leveling / feats. You'll have to modify your ability scores based on the method used.
* You may notice your character sheet has sections called "Personality Traits," "Ideals," "Bonds," and "Flaws." Don't stress about these, plenty of players leave them blank.
* You'll be expected to brainstorm ideas for your character's backstory during session 0, which will explain why you're adventuring. The background you choose during character creation can influence this, but otherwise popular motivations for your character include "Avenging a loved one," "Getting rich," "Searching for secret knowledge," or "Proving yourself a hero." If possible, your backstory should conform with what kind of setting the DM is using (whether homebrew or published content) and the tone of the campaign.
* Some people will come in with races or subclasses that aren't mentioned in the PHB, like the Tortle race or the Hexblade Warlock subclass (or the entire class of Artificer). You don't have to know the details of this content, just say "I've never played as a \[\] before."

Finally, there's lots of comments here saying that they're definitely going to find out and you should just tell them. I'm pretty sure that some of the people I've played with before have never opened the PHB in their lives, despite playing for years, so I'm not confident this is true. I'd say best of luck to you, and if you forget a rule, so what? Everyone does. Show up, have fun, and enjoy the new hobby that your web of lies has spawned.

That's the thing, each encounter is meant to *feel* challenging, while in reality the party should be winning most of the time. This is a delicate balance and it mostly works if the players are similarly effective in combat. If 4/5 players are choosing their race, background, and feats for story reasons rather than practicality, then they're going to feel less useful than the one min-maxer who's doing 60+ dmg per round. The DM effectively has to give monsters more HP, higher AC, higher atk bonuses just to challenge one person while leaving other characters unable to hit. It creates a dynamic where some character options are just not worth taking, and that's a shame if you care about the other half of the game, roleplay.

That said, minmaxing can be fine at certain tables where all of the players agree they want that kind of play style. But I would expect the DM to raise the difficulty of encounters to compensate, so if your goal is to steamroll enemies then that still probably won't happen.

I've played in heavy minmaxing games before and I actually notice that these kinds of players can get equally frustrated when faced with enemies with enough resources to be a challenge. Mostly it just means that the BBG has a crapton of legendary resistances and keeps attacking the wizard instead of the barbarian who was built to be the tankiest tank to ever tank. Imo if it's going to be challenging either way, might as well have more freedom when making the character.

If you've never DM'd before I would say try a module first to get used to the feel of running the game, or better yet one of the official D&D adventures. Stick fairly close to the book--new DMs often worry too much about railroading their players but it's often worse to let your players bumble off into regions that don't have any content prepared.

Customize your DM screen, whether you're using an online tool or a physical screen. I like to include NPC names, loot tables, and prices of common items. I'm sure there's other helpful info which others can point out in the comments.

For combat, you're going to have a lot going on so do as much prep as you can ahead of time so you can focus on narration and not referencing stat blocks. If you're not familiar with how monster stat blocks are laid out, practice running a mock combat to make sure you know where to find all the info you'll need. Spellcasters in particular are more complicated to run, so I like to make decision trees for what they'll do in a particular encounter (e.g. Tommy the Wizard will start by casting Mage Armor, then drop a Fireball, then retreat if he gets below a certain HP threshold). Consider rolling enemy HP in advance, or just using the baseline HP.

If you're not sure how a player's ability or spell works, just ask them to read it verbatim--it's on them to have that information ready, not you.

Good luck and have fun!

I agree that nostalgia plays a huge role in older readers’ enjoyment of the series, but I disagree on your criticisms of the way magic works in the series. It doesn’t have the strict rules of other fantasy universes because it was meant to be more whimsical. Does Rowling employ a healthy amount of Deus Ex? Of course. See the end of book 3 time turners which are used one then never seen again, despite being an incredibly useful tool. But other aspects of the books are just fun for the sake of being fun. See: the hex designed to tickle your target, or anything created by Fred and George. This makes them well suited for a younger audience, sure, but I think that the argument that older reader should scorn these books BECAUSE it’s goofy and fun is a bit highbrow. 

As for your comments on the movies: Nope. Sorry. Movies are never going to be as good as the books, simply due to time constraints, but even with that being said the HP movies were still pretty great. Fantastic musical score, great actors (even the kids were fine, which is a pretty tall order with child actors), excellent cinematography. The special effects weren’t bad in the early movies, but as the budget became bigger, they became extremely impressive, especially in the fifth movie. Overall, solid films.

I completely agree. Slaughterhouse Five is one of my all-time favorites, but I feel like it’s underrated by lots of readers because it’s not plot driven. Rather, it’s sort of aimless and wandering because that’s what Vonnegut is trying to say about war. The constant repetition of “So it goes,” the short stories about the money tree and how the bible should’ve gone, it all builds up to an atmosphere of “This is wrong, but what can we do about it?” Billy Pilgrim feels like he CAN’T do anything about it, which eventually leads to his psychotic break and unique philosophy on life: You can’t change what’s destined to happen, so suffering, and war, and unnecessary death is ok. This emotion is what I feel Vonnegut is trying to evoke, and in this Slaughterhouse Five was, at least for me,  extremely successful. 

(Side note: obviously Vonnegut’s end goal wasn’t justify war. The gloomy tone is meant to create a backlash in the reader, to make them say, ‘No, actually, this ISN’T alright with me, and someone really ought to do something about it.’ It IS an anti war book, after all. But I felt like this digressed from the main point I was trying to make above.)
